name: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol
statement: Fetch web resources through stateless request-and-response messages between a client and a server.
statementAccent: stateless request-and-response messages between a client and a server
meaning: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, or HTTP, is an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite and the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web, used for fetching resources such as HTML documents. It is a request-response protocol in the client-server model: a client, typically a web browser, sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server returns an HTTP response. HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning each request is independent and the server does not by itself retain state between requests; state, such as a logged-in session, is added on top through mechanisms like cookies. HTTP defines request methods, or verbs, indicating the desired action: GET retrieves a resource, POST submits data, and others include PUT, DELETE, and HEAD. Every response carries a status code indicating the result, grouped by the first digit: 1xx informational, 2xx success such as 200 OK, 3xx redirection such as 301 and 302, 4xx client errors such as 404 Not Found and 403 Forbidden, and 5xx server errors such as 500 Internal Server Error. HTTP typically runs over TCP, traditionally on port 80, while HTTPS is HTTP secured with TLS, encrypting the traffic, on port 443. HTTP was initiated by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN around 1989 to 1991, beginning with the simple HTTP/0.9, followed by HTTP/1.0 in 1996 and HTTP/1.1, and later by HTTP/2 in 2015, which is binary and multiplexed, and HTTP/3, which runs over QUIC and UDP. It is the protocol of the Web.
mechanism: HTTP structures communication on the Web as a simple exchange: a client asks for something, and a server answers. Every interaction is a request paired with a response, framed in the client-server model where browsers, apps, and other clients initiate and servers respond. A request names a method, or verb, that says what the client wants done, most commonly GET to retrieve a resource identified by a URL, POST to submit data such as a form, and others like PUT to store, DELETE to remove, and HEAD to fetch only headers; it also carries headers with metadata and, sometimes, a body. The server processes the request and returns a response consisting of a status code, response headers, and usually a body containing the requested resource. The status code, a three-digit number grouped by its first digit, tells the client what happened: 1xx informational, 2xx success like the familiar 200 OK, 3xx redirection like 301 and 302 pointing elsewhere, 4xx client errors like 404 Not Found when a resource is missing or 403 Forbidden when access is denied, and 5xx server errors like 500 Internal Server Error. A defining property is statelessness: HTTP treats each request as self-contained, with the server keeping no memory of previous requests on its own, which keeps the protocol simple and scalable; applications that need continuity, like shopping carts or logins, layer state on top using cookies and sessions. HTTP messages are carried over a reliable transport, historically TCP on port 80, and HTTPS wraps HTTP inside TLS for encryption and authentication on port 443, now the norm. From Tim Berners-Lee's original HTTP at CERN, the protocol evolved through HTTP/1.1 to the binary, multiplexed HTTP/2 and the QUIC-based HTTP/3, improving performance while keeping the request-response model.

whyItMatters: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol is the language of the Web, the protocol over which nearly all of the world's web traffic flows, and it is one of the foundational inventions of the modern Internet. When Tim Berners-Lee created HTTP at CERN around 1990 alongside HTML and the URL, he established the simple, powerful pattern that still governs the Web: a client requests a resource by its address, and a server responds with it. That request-response model, combined with statelessness, proved extraordinarily scalable, letting web servers handle vast numbers of independent requests without tracking each client, and it became the substrate not only for browsing pages but for the entire ecosystem of web applications, APIs, and services that dominate computing today. HTTP's vocabulary, its methods like GET and POST and its status codes like 200, 404, and 500, is so pervasive that it has entered common culture, and its secured form HTTPS, HTTP wrapped in TLS, now protects the overwhelming majority of web traffic, safeguarding privacy and trust online. The protocol has continually evolved to meet the Web's growth, from HTTP/1.1 to the multiplexed HTTP/2 and the QUIC-based HTTP/3, each improving speed while preserving the familiar model. As the stateless request-response protocol that fetches the resources of the Web, HTTP is essential to how billions of people use the Internet every day.

working.text: the client sends an HTTP request naming a method like GET and a resource to a server.
the server replies with a status code and, usually, the requested resource.
since HTTP is stateless, use cookies and sessions to maintain continuity like logins across requests.

limits: HTTP is the Web's foundation, but its design choices carry limits that reward care. Its statelessness, essential to scalability, means the protocol itself remembers nothing between requests, so any continuity, logins, shopping carts, personalization, must be built on top with cookies, sessions, or tokens, and treating HTTP as inherently stateful is a mistake. Plain HTTP provides no security: it transmits data in the clear, so it can be read or tampered with in transit, which is why HTTPS, HTTP over TLS, is now essential and standard, and unencrypted HTTP is deprecated for anything sensitive. The classic request-response model is client-initiated, so the server cannot on its own push data to the client, a limitation that spawned workarounds and complementary technologies like WebSockets for real-time communication. Performance limitations of older versions, such as HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking, drove the development of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Some historical and technical details reward care: HTTP is an application-layer protocol usually running over TCP on port 80, with HTTPS on 443; it was initiated by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, with development beginning in 1989 and HTTP/0.9 dating to 1991; and HTTP/2 dates to 2015 and HTTP/3 to 2022. So HTTP robustly fetches web resources by request and response, understood as stateless, insecure without TLS, and client-initiated by design.
misreadings: HTTP is not stateful; it remembers nothing between requests, and continuity comes from cookies and sessions. Plain HTTP is not secure, so HTTPS with TLS is needed for privacy. And its request-response model is client-initiated, not server-push, so treating HTTP as stateful, as secure by itself, or as able to push data unprompted, misreads it.
origin: The application-layer protocol of the Web, initiated by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN around 1989 to 1991, which fetches resources through stateless request-and-response messages between clients and servers.
